question:
Patient note:
A 99-year-old man, a retired railroad signal engineer who still spends most afternoons repairing vintage pocket watches at his kitchen table, was brought to the geriatric medicine office by his grandson for evaluation of progressive leg discomfort during ambulation and review of his respiratory and metabolic conditions before the family arranges a move across the country so that he can live closer to great-grandchildren. The patient ambulated from the parking lot with a rollator but reported that over the past year the distance he can cover before his calves seize with a cramp-like pressure has fallen from three city blocks to less than half a block; the pain resolves within two minutes of standing still and has never occurred while he is seated. A vascular study performed three months ago documented ankle–brachial indices of 0.52 on the right and 0.50 on the left with monophasic waveforms in the posterior tibial arteries. He has never developed ulceration, rest pain, or gangrene, but he does note that the skin over both shins has become shiny and sparsely haired. Respiratory history is significant for a 75-pack-year cigarette exposure that ended when he turned 82, after an admission for influenza complicated by an acute exacerbation of underlying airflow limitation. Post-bronchodilator spirometry obtained last winter revealed an FEV1 of 0.9 L (38 % predicted) and an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.44 with negligible reversibility; he uses a once-daily tiotropium capsule and a budesonide-formoterol inhaler twice daily, consuming a canister of rescue albuterol roughly every six weeks, and has required two five-day prednisone tapers during the past 12 months but no mechanical ventilation or domiciliary oxygen. This morning he speaks in full sentences, respiratory rate is 18 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation is 93 % on ambient air, dipping to 90 % after a sixty-second corridor walk and recovering within two minutes of rest. Metabolic history reveals that he was diagnosed with diabetes 30 years ago; despite glipizide and lifestyle counseling, his glycated hemoglobin has hovered near 8 % for many years. Ten years ago an ophthalmologist documented microaneurysms and cotton-wool spots consistent with background retinopathy, and last month’s dilated exam noted mild macular edema though visual acuity remains 20/40 bilaterally. Neurologically he describes a stocking distribution tingling that obliges him to test bathwater temperature with his elbow; monofilament testing by the visiting nurse service is frequently diminished at the great toes. Urine microalbumin-to-creatinine ratio measured two weeks ago was 210 mg/g, but serum creatinine remains 1.0 mg/dL with an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 68 mL/min/1.73 m². He has never required dialysis or nephrology referral. Two years ago he underwent excisional biopsy of a slowly enlarging right cervical node; pathology demonstrated a low-grade follicular B-cell lymphoma, Ann Arbor stage II, and the hematology team elected watchful waiting in light of the patient’s age, small volume of adenopathy, and absence of B symptoms. Over the ensuing period he has maintained stable node size on serial ultrasound, denies fevers, drenching night sweats, or unintentional weight loss, and hemoglobin today is 11.8 g/dL, down only slightly from baseline. Cardiac review is unremarkable: he denies squeezing chest pain, diaphoresis, orthopnea, or lower-extremity swelling, and an echocardiogram last year showed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 62 % with no regional wall-motion abnormalities or valvular pathology. He also denies sudden unilateral weakness, slurred speech, facial droop, or transient visual loss at any point. Gastrointestinal review is notable only for constipation managed with prunes; he has never experienced dyspepsia, hematemesis, black stools, or been told of peptic ulcers. He abstains from alcohol except for a small champagne toast at family weddings, and liver enzymes obtained last week were alanine aminotransferase 26 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 28 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 74 U/L, total bilirubin 0.6 mg/dL, albumin 3.9 g/dL, and international normalized ratio 1.1. Current medications include tiotropium 18 µg inhaled each morning, budesonide-formoterol 160/4.5 µg two inhalations twice daily, albuterol metered-dose inhaler as needed, metformin 500 mg twice daily, glipizide 10 mg with breakfast, aspirin 81 mg daily, atorvastatin 10 mg nightly, and a timed-release gabapentin capsule 300 mg at bedtime for neuropathic discomfort; he reports no drug allergies. Vital signs today: temperature 36.7 °C, blood pressure 128/66 mm Hg seated in the left arm, pulse 72 beats/min regular, respiratory rate as noted, weight 58 kg, height 172 cm, body-mass index 19.6 kg/m². He is alert, oriented, and recounts World War II rail schedules with striking accuracy. Conjunctivae are pink, sclerae anicteric; pupils equal and reactive, no xanthelasma. Neck is supple without JVP elevation or carotid bruit; scattered 1-cm mobile, non-tender nodes are palpated in the right posterior cervical chain. Cardiac point of maximal impulse is nondisplaced, S1 and S2 are crisp without murmurs, rubs, or gallops. Lungs reveal diminished breath sounds diffusely, prolonged expiration with end-expiratory wheezes, and faint bibasilar crackles but no egophony. Abdomen is flat and soft with normal bowel tones, liver edge smooth and palpable 1 cm below the costal margin, spleen not felt, no ascites. Examination of the lower extremities shows cool feet, hair loss below the knees, capillary refill of six seconds at the great toes, 1+ edema at the ankles, femoral pulses 1+/4, popliteal pulses absent to palpation but Doppler audible, and dorsalis pedis signals monophasic; dependent rubor develops after the feet are dangled for thirty seconds. Sensation to light touch is reduced over the distal feet, vibration sense absent at the halluces, and proprioception is mildly impaired, though motor strength remains 5/5 throughout and Romberg testing is negative; gait is slow and shuffling, limited primarily by calf discomfort. A portable spirometer in clinic records FEV1 0.88 L, FVC 1.94 L, and FEV1/FVC 0.45 consistent with obstructive physiology unchanged from prior. Twelve-lead electrocardiogram shows normal sinus rhythm at 70 beats/min, axis 20°, PR interval 160 ms, QRS 90 ms, no Q waves, and nonspecific ST-T changes identical to tracings from two years ago. Chest radiograph reveals hyperinflated lungs with flattened diaphragms and no focal consolidation. The family seeks guidance regarding the risks of cross-country relocation, optimization of walking capacity, safety of continued observation for his lymphoma, and inhaler adjustments for elevation change in the new residence.

Question: What is the patient's Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The age-adjusted Charlson Comorbidity Index adds age points to the weights for qualifying chronic diseases.
- Age (<50 = 0, 50–59 = 1, 60–69 = 2, 70–79 = 3, ≥80 = 4): age 99 = 4.
- Peripheral vascular disease: exertional calf claudication relieved by rest and ankle–brachial indices of 0.50–0.52 confirm symptomatic peripheral artery disease = 1.
- Chronic pulmonary disease: COPD with persistent airflow obstruction on post-bronchodilator spirometry = 1.
- Diabetes with end-organ damage: documented diabetic retinopathy qualifies = 2. Neuropathy and albuminuria do not add further diabetes points, and uncomplicated diabetes is not scored separately.
- Lymphoma: biopsy-confirmed follicular B-cell lymphoma qualifies even under observation = 2.
- Other qualifying comorbidities = 0. Albuminuria with creatinine 1.0 mg/dL and eGFR 68 does not meet the separate moderate-to-severe renal disease criterion.
Total: 4 + 1 + 1 + 2 + 2 + 0 = 10.
Final answer: 10
